2026-10-10 XMPP and OMEMO

2026-10-10

2026-10-10 XMPP and OMEMO

There’s this joke about the various encrypted messengers that basically goes like this: you open the messenger app and all you can see is that all your chats are encrypted and your device cannot decrypt them anymore.

Encryption is hard, and the usability around it is hard, too.

I have Prosody running as the XMPP server and on the little laptop I wanted to use Profanity as the text user interface (TUI) client. It looks a lot like irssi for IRC. Weird, but OK. And it seems to work just fine, except encryption does not.

If I understand this correctly, all that is required from me is to run /omemo gen and within a few seconds I should be ready to go, showing fingerprints, trusting them, and so on. But that’s not what’s happening. Instead, a few seconds after generating whatever the command generates, I get a message, about three or four times per second (!), saying: “Could not find own OMEMO device ID. Going to publish own device ID: 1579300267”. Why is it doing that? How can I stop it? Is this a bug in Profanity, in Prosody, in my configs, or what? I have no idea.

#XMPP

2026-10-10. I got an interesting pointer on the Profanity channel: commit bbd9442db from June this year.

fix: query bare JID for PEP features during discovery

XEP-0163 (Personal Eventing Protocol) states that service discovery information queries regarding PEP capabilities must be sent to the users bare JID in order to determine support.

Profanity only queried the server domain JID and its generic disco#items on connect, but never queried the users own bare JID.

Because ejabberd advertises PEP and PubSub features on both the server JID and the bare JID this bug was kind of invisible. However, Prosody strictly advertises PEP capabilities only on the users bare JID.

This discovery failure became a hard blocker for OMEMO on Prosody servers following commit 01c781fcf (“Don’t publish keys if the server doesn’t support pubsub.”), which turned the check for publish-options into an early-return condition.

We now query our own bare JID during feature discovery on connect and insert it into conn.features_by_jid.

I now have a build with that patch and it seems to work!

Install tools:

sudo apt install dpkg-dev devscripts

Add a deb-src section to /etc/apt/sources.list.d/debian.sources:

Types: deb-src
URIs: http://deb.debian.org/debian/
Suites: unstable
Components: main contrib non-free
Signed-By: /usr/share/keyrings/debian-archive-keyring.gpg

Update packages and install the build dependencies:

sudo apt update
sudo apt build-dep profanity

Find an empty directory and get the Debian sources and get the current sources:

mkdir profanity-build
cd profanity-build
sudo apt source profanity
git clone git@github.com:profanity-im/profanity.git

Now get the patch from the current sources and apply it to the Debian sources:

cd profanity
git format-patch bbd9442db^..bbd9442db
cd ../profanity-0.18.2
patch -p1 < ../profanity/0001-fix-query-bare-JID-for-PEP-features-during-discovery.patch

Build and install it:

debuild -i -us -uc -b
cd ..
sudo dpkg -i profanity_0.18.2-1_arm64.deb

Testing it: In Profanity, run /omemo gen and you should be able to use it as documented.

There's little that's "inevitable" about AI

2026-10-10

The glib response here would be to say that no technology is ever inevitable and that everything is contingent. This has the advantages of being technically true and sounding wise, but unfortunately technologies very much exist that a reasonable person might well label that way. Firearms are a good example of the latter case: once they've been developed, you quite quickly hit the situation where if you want to maintain your independence and safety in a society, you have to either use one or have one used on your behalf: no other options really work.

Friday Squid Blogging: I Caught a Squid

2026-10-09

On Wednesday I spent a day fishing, on a small boat out of Gloucester, MA. We caught many cod (none of which we could keep), and a bunch of hake and mackerel (all of which we could keep). And…I caught a squid! Near as I can tell, it’s a longfin squid, sometimes called a Boston squid ( Doryteuthis (Amerigo) pealeii).

That night I cooked it over a barbecue grill—hot and fast. Delicious.

Pluralistic: Thwarted (09 Oct 2026)

2026-10-09

Today's links Thwarted: Behold the awesome destructive power of a fully operational billionaire. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Anthrax v National Inquirer; Grey goo v Second Life; Predictive policing v actual crime; Spooky cookies; California v algorithmic price-fixing; Tivo self-destructs; Disney exec endorses piracy; TSA v geologists; Handheld printer; Mandatory DRM for all Canadian music sales; Iceweasel; "Snuff"; "Shade the Changing Girl"; Latam surveillance; Scotland Yard brands encryption terrorism; RBS slaughtered 10k small businesses to seize and sell their assets; Dead Letters. Upcoming appearances: Calgary, Winnipeg, Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Kilkenny, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Thwarted (permalink) There are many ways in which every billionaire is a policy failure, but the most corrosive and destructive way in which billionaires are policy failures is this: billionaires, despite being unelected and unaccountable, possess the power to control – and ruin – millions of peoples' lives. Despite what the Prosperity Gospel and the Efficient Market Hypothesis would have you believe, having billions of dollars is in no way a reliable predictor that you also possess the wisdom to unilaterally dictate how thousands or millions of other people must live their lives, and that dictatorial power is most the tangible effect of being a billionaire. Billionaireism is many things, but above all else, it is the power to do whatever *you* want to do, at the expense of whatever *other* people want to do. To be a billionaire is to live a life unthwarted, above the power of your workers, your neighbors, or your government and its laws. It is the right to get high on your own supply. It is the right to live a life in which no one ever calls you on your bullshit. Billionaires aspire to live a one-sided libertarian fantasy in which they have the unlimited right to do whatever they want, and *you* have the right to do whatever they tell you to do. There has always been a group of people who refused to acknowledge that other people have perfectly valid reasons for wanting to pursue their own goals rather than theirs. We call most of those people "toddlers" and devote sizable social effort to helping them outgrow this belief. Billionaires, on the other hand, command resources that allow *them* to devote sizable effort to getting *us* to acknowledge that *they* should be able to tell *us* what to do. This is why billionaires love neoclassical economics, with its doctrine of "revealed preferences," which holds that the only true way to understand someone's preferences is to ignore what they *say* and only pay attention to what they *do*. It's a belief that can only be adopted by people who suffer the self-inflicted neurological injury you get from doing an economics degree, which renders the victim incapable of perceiving or reasoning about power. To believe in "revealed preferences" is to observe someone who has sold their kidney to pay the rent and marvel at this person who has a revealed preference for only having one kidney: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/30/players-of-games/#know-when-to-fold-em "Revealed preferences" is the economist's version of the bully who grabs your arm and starts whacking you with your own hand while shouting, "stop hitting yourself!" The ideological purpose that "revealed preferences" fills is letting billionaires live a life unthwarted. It's a life where they thwart everyone else, but still claim to be believers in "freedom." This is what Peter Thiel meant when he wrote that "democracy is incompatible with freedom." In a democracy, the people who you exercise coercive power over are able to band together to create public institutions that act as a check on your power. For Thiel to maximize his freedom (to do things like spying on us and crushing our journalistic outlets), he must prevent all of *us* from voting, lest we vote to take away those cherished freedoms of his: https://www.cato-unbound.org/2009/04/13/peter-thiel/education-libertarian/ We're told that as mere mortals, we must inevitably submit to "death and taxes." Billionaires have long since so corrupted our political system that they need not pay taxes: https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/S/bo256019296.html They have (practically speaking) infinite wealth, which means that they have practically infinite power, including the power to block any democratic attempt to limit their wealth (and thus their power): https://www.hamiltonnolan.com/p/the-war-against-accumulated-capital Having vanquished taxes, the ultra-rich are now committed to defeating death as well, making themselves easy marks for the world's weirdest cult leaders and grifters, who promise them a mix of physical and digital immortality: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0oVSnaINJ30 The fact that billionaires are such suckers, so often, is the strongest argument against billionaireism. Billionaires aren't just powerful, they're also *fallible*. We're *all* fallible, of course, but only billionaires get to impose their foolish ideas on so many other people, who have no say in the matter. Henry Ford thought that he was so rich that he could build Brazilian worker housing whose windows faced the same direction as the worker housing he'd built in Dearborn, Michigan. He literally thought that being rich meant that he could ignore the entire concept of *the Earth's axial tilt* (he was wrong): https://memex.craphound.com/2010/06/02/fordlandia-novelistic-history-of-henry-fords-doomed-midwestern-town-in-the-amazon-jungle/ Of course that was the least of Ford's follies. Ford also believed in a secret Jewish conspiracy to control humanity: https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/henryford-antisemitism/ And despite the fact that Ford was so often demonstrably as thick as pigshit, no one was able to stop him from hiring soldiers to literally slaughter anyone who tried to limit his ability to tell other people how to live their lives: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Overpass Ford is no exception. Elon Musk believes in the same racist garbage as Henry Ford…but he also believes that if you're rich enough, you can simply wish away *geometry* and *physics*: https://pluralistic.net/2025/07/24/geometry-hates-cars/#dogshit-unit-economics More than anyone else, Musk illustrates the way that being insulated from people who can thwart you leads to absolute ruination. Every terrible idea Musk has, he gets to act on. This has all kinds of negative impacts, including the very real possibility that some day your house will be crushed by his flaming rocketry debris: https://www.vice.com/en/article/texas-residents-are-suing-spacex-over-terrestrial-bombardment/ That's small potatoes, though: Musk's wrong ideas, combined with his billionaire's impunity, also allowed him to murder hundreds of thousands of the world's poorest children: https://hsph.harvard.edu/news/usaid-shutdown-has-led-to-hundreds-of-thousands-of-deaths/ Billionaireism is fractally terrible. By definition, the kind of person who will inflict the kinds of harms needed to amass billions of dollars in pursuit of total impunity is someone who will use that impunity to hurt even more people. Anyone who fails to outgrow a toddler's insistence on subordinating others to their will *should not be allowed to subordinate anyone to their will*. Billionaire dilettantes aren't like regular dilettantes. Anyone can be a crank, but billionaire cranks have the force-multiplier of money and the impunity it brings. These allow a billionaire to turn his crackpot ideas into an unstoppable force that crushes public education: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/09/autocrats-of-trade-2/#witness-the-firepower-of-this-fully-armed-and-operational-battle-station It also lets billionaires (including the billionaire ruining public education) kidnap and rape more than a thousand girls on a private island: https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/what-to-know-about-bill-gates-relationship-with-jeffrey-epstein-as-he-is-interviewed-in-house-probe Whatever crank whim a rich person has, we all have to live with. Take Barre Seid: the 94 year old billionaire made his fortune manufacturing electronics, and then donated $1.6b to fund "attack philanthropy" in order to undermine belief in climate change and prevent any action from being taken to avert it: https://www.propublica.org/article/barre-seid-heartland-institute-hillsdale-college-gmu Seid is one of the main reasons we're experiencing the super El Nino. He's not just in the top 0.1% of wealth-horders, he's also in the top 0.1% of people we can blame for the *twelve foot sea-level rise* that is currently wiping Long Beach off the map: https://ktla.com/news/local-news/long-beach-boardwalk-collapse-rachel-surf/ Henry Ford didn't believe in the planet's axial tilt. Elon Musk doesn't believe in geometry. Barre Seid doesn't believe in climate change. But Barre Seid *does* believe something: Barre Seid believes in *rats*. For *three years*, Seid has paid a small army of goons to wander the area around Chicago's Lincoln Park, scattering handfuls of high-grade nuts on the ground, which have drawn flocks of pigeons and swarms of rats. Rats are everywhere. Everything is covered in pigeon shit. Seid has been repeatedly fined and cited and warned, and he's carried on turning the neighborhood into an uncontrolled vermin breeding facility: https://gizmodo.com/a-billionaire-is-fueling-a-rat-explosion-in-a-chicago-park-in-the-stupidest-way-possible-2000823641 Whether or not the people who live, work and play in Lincoln Park want to be swarmed by rats and slip in thick slicks of pigeon shit is irrelevant. Seid can afford to pay any fine the city levies against him (a fine is a price, and he's a billionaire), which means there's no practical reason Seid has to ever stop. He has the freedom to operate unthwarted in his every desire, including his desire to carpet an entire neighborhood in feces, so everyone else lacks the freedom to live without pigeon shit and rats. That's the thing about billionaires: as Peter Thiel wrote, democracy *is* incompatible with freedom (to be a billionaire). The fact that Barre Seid's desire to transform Lincoln Park into a pigeon-shit manure lagoon is wildly unpopular with Chicagoans is irrelevant. You can't vote Barre Seid out of office, because no one elected him Pigeon Shit Czar. He has assumed that office by right of conquest. Our lives are full of horrible, extremely unpopular things that we can't vote away because billionaires like them. Take the decision to allow Larry Ellison and his failson to buy and kill Warner Studios. That's an incredibly unpopular idea, especially in California, where Warner, Paramount and the Ellisons are all based. Despite the fact that we all hate this idea, Ellison gets to do it, because he is unthwartable: https://pluralistic.net/2026/09/22/happy-chudmas/#baloney-in-our-slacks Some of California's most powerful Democrats promised to stop the merger. Instead, they signed away California's future because they decided that they weren't powerful enough to thwart a billionaire: https://prospect.org/2026/10/08/democrats-who-let-trumps-oligarchs-buy-hollywood-warner-bros-david-ellison-gavin-newsom/ The Warnermount disaster demonstrates the fundamental flaw in libertarianism. Even if you're the kind of Musk-addled libertarian who can't open your copy of *Atlas Shrugged* anymore because the pages are all stuck together and you think the only role for the state is enforcing contracts, you *still need the state to be able to enforce those contracts*. If corporations or even individual billionaires amass more power than the state, then they can always tell the state's contract enforcers to fuck off. The ref must be more powerful than the players on the field, so the smallest government you can have is determined by the size of the largest corporation and the wealth of the richest billionaire you're willing to tolerate. The world is in *really* bad shape right now, but it doesn't have to be. As Mamdani has shown us, it's not that hard to run a well-administered, advanced technological civilization. Fixing potholes and making transit work and enforcing housing rules isn't rocket surgery. We know how to do those things – we just don't do them because billionaires don't want us to, and they are unthwartable: https://yourlocalepidemiologist.substack.com/p/the-revolutionary-art-of-fixing-the We let the most greedy, most ruthless people among us pursue their toddler's quest for an unthwarted life to the expense of any semblance of competent administration, and now we are *fucked*. That's why people are so angry about AI: there's nothing wrong with the idea of automating some tasks through advanced statistical techniques, but the reason so much of the world's scarce resources have been allocated to the AI buildout is that billionaires are infinitely horny for a technology that will let them sideline expertise in favor of money: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/06/nonfungible/#theory-free After all, experts get to thwart billionaires. They can refuse to apply their expertise to a billionaire's folly. The kind of AI that the industry is pursuing today is predicated on the idea that you can just ask a computer to come up with "theory-free inferences" that will let it run a factory, drive a car, or perform medicine, without knowing *anything*, just by pulling statistical correlations out of unimaginably vast data-sets. At some level, people get this. They understand that AI and billionaireism are intimately connected – that the reason the sector is on track to lose about a trillion dollars this year is that for billionaires, a trillion bucks is a small price to pay for an unthwartable life. A Simple Overview of LLM Sampling Methods

2026-10-09, updated: 2026-10-10

A Simple Overview of LLM Sampling Methods

Almost all the dis­course around LLMs to­day is cen­tered on the mod­els them­selves. This model is bet­ter than that model which is bet­ter than this other model. It’s… ex­haust­ing. It’s also barely scratch­ing the sur­face of what makes an ef­fec­tive LLM-based sys­tem.

Today, I want to in­tro­duce you to an en­tirely new world. The world of sam­pling al­go­rithms. We’ll dis­cuss what they are, how some of them work, and the im­pact they can have on sys­tem per­for­mance.

What Is a Sampling Algorithm?

If you’ve re­ceived even a sim­ple ex­pla­na­tion of how au­tore­gres­sive lan­guage mod­els work, you likely al­ready have an in­tu­itive un­der­stand­ing of what a sam­pling al­go­rithm is. If you have not, do not worry. It is not ac­tu­ally as com­plex as it sounds.

When you give an LLM a piece of text, it does­n’t ac­tu­ally spit out more text. The act of“writing” as­so­ci­ated with LLMs when used in chat­bots or else­where comes from a higher or­der pro­gram that sim­ply uses an LLM. The LLM it­self is only ca­pa­ble of spit­ting out a prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion.

What dis­tri­b­u­tion might that be? Given a se­quence of words, an LLM emits the prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion of what word might come next.

I talk about this in more depth in my blog post about Markov Chains.

For ex­am­ple, let’s say we of­fer an LLM the phrase,“The cat sat on the”. In re­turn, the LLM will give us a prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion over all the pos­si­ble words that might come next.

WordProbabilityhat0.9bat0.05ra­di­a­tor0.04…0.01

In or­der to gen­er­ate text, all we need to do is choose among these pos­si­ble words and ap­pend it to our in­put. From there, we may re­peat the cy­cle all over again. If we do this enough times, we can get co­her­ent-sound­ing prose from the model.

Here’s the hard part: How we do choose a word from the prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion? The an­swer: Use a sam­pling al­go­rithm.

Greedy Sampling.

Greedy sam­pling is the most ob­vi­ous so­lu­tion. Given a prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion, a greedy sam­pling al­go­rithm will sim­ply choose the most likely word every time.

In our“The cat sat on the” ex­am­ple, our greedy al­go­rithm would choose the most prob­a­ble word,“hat”. It’s sim­ple, el­e­gant, and it can some­times get the job done. But, as you may have guessed, it is not op­ti­mal.

The most ob­vi­ous prob­lem with greedy sam­pling ap­pears as soon as you gen­er­ate a mean­ing­ful amount of text. It’s ﬁlled with rep­e­ti­tions.

When I ask a small lan­guage model like SmolLM2:135M about Python, I get:

Python is a great lan­guage for be­gin­ners, as it’s easy to learn and has a large com­mu­nity of users. However, it’s worth not­ing that Python can be chal­leng­ing to learn, es­pe­cially for those with­out prior ex­pe­ri­ence with pro­gram­ming. But with the right re­sources and a solid foun­da­tion, Python can be a pow­er­ful tool for any­one look­ing to de­velop in­no­v­a­tive so­lu­tions.

Some of the key fea­tures of Python in­clude:

  • Python 3.x: Python 3.x is the lat­est ver­sion of Python, which is widely used in the in­dus­try.
  • Standard Library: Python has a large stan­dard li­brary that in­cludes a wide range of tools and func­tions for var­i­ous tasks.
  • Extensive Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): Python has a strong fo­cus on OOP, mak­ing it suit­able for build­ing com­plex ap­pli­ca­tions and sys­tems.
  • Cross-Platform: Python can run on mul­ti­ple plat­forms, in­clud­ing Windows, ma­cOS, Linux, and Android.
  • Cross-Platform: Python can run on mul­ti­ple plat­forms, in­clud­ing Windows, ma­cOS, Linux, and Android.

Notice any­thing?

Most ob­vi­ously, it re­peats it­self un­nec­es­sar­ily. It men­tions“Cross-Platform” twice, with the same de­scrip­tion text. It’s only a mi­nor an­noy­ance here, but rep­e­ti­tion like this can be dev­as­tat­ing for long-con­text rea­son­ing mod­els. Us­ing a sam­pling al­go­rithm that is“too greedy” is a com­mon rea­son for“looping” be­hav­ior in off-the-shelf rea­son­ing mod­els when they are set up in­cor­rectly.

Additionally, the model ﬁnds it­self too ad­her­ent to its own train­ing data. No­tice how it lists“Python 3.x” as a“feature” of the lan­guage? This is be­cause that par­tic­u­lar Python ver­sion num­ber ap­pears fre­quently in the data. That means it can get ranked at the top of the prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion, even if it has noth­ing to do with the sur­round­ing con­text.

Okay, how can we ﬁx these prob­lems?

Statistical Sampling

The sec­ond most ob­vi­ous sam­pling method is to sam­ple from the prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion ran­domly. Let’s pull up that dis­tri­b­u­tion from ear­lier:

WordProbabilityhat0.9bat0.05ra­di­a­tor0.04…0.01

Our model sug­gests that the ﬁrst word,“hat” is 18 times more likely to be the next word. In sta­tis­ti­cal sam­pling, we honor that. In­stead of only sam­pling the most likely word like in greedy sam­pling, in sta­tis­ti­cal sam­pling we sam­ple ran­domly, bi­as­ing our­selves to sam­ple the more likely words more of­ten.

The sim­plest al­go­rithm to ac­com­plish this is to:

  1. Generate a ran­dom num­ber rrr be­tween 0 and 1.
  2. Iterate through the prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion pip_ipi​, start­ing with the most prob­a­ble word ﬁrst.
  3. Once we en­counter a word pxp_xpx​ such that ∑n=1xpn>=r\sum_{n = 1}^{x} p_n >= r∑n=1x​pn​>=r, we sam­ple it.

In prac­tice, this leads to more var­ied text. The model no longer needs to stick to the most likely word. In­stead, we can oc­ca­sion­ally dip down and emit the less likely (potentially more in­ter­est­ing) words.

In rea­son­ing mod­els, this al­lows the model to ex­plore more cre­ative so­lu­tions to prob­lems. Sta­tis­ti­cal sam­pling (and the vari­ants we ex­plore be­low) also mit­i­gate the rep­e­ti­tion we saw in the greedy al­go­rithm.

One of the prob­lems with sta­tis­tic sam­pling is that the ran­dom­ness can oc­ca­sion­ally pro­duce words that are en­tirely un­re­lated to the topic at hand.

By us­ing a rather ag­gres­sive sta­tis­ti­cal sam­pler with the same model as be­fore, we get some­thing that seems ﬁne at ﬁrst, but de­grades rather quickly.

Python is an in­ter­preted, dy­nam­i­cally-typed pro­gram­ming lan­guage cre­ated by Guido van Rossum. Its core fea­tures in­clude syn­tax for com­pact read­able code, ease of use with vast li­braries and mod­ules, good per­for­mance, ease of de­vel­op­ment with con­ve­nient de­vel­op­ment en­vi­ron­ments, user-friendly GUI, seam­less in­ter­ac­tions with on­line ser­vices, se­cure web cod­ing, and data­bases for seam­less busi­ness pro­duc­tiv­ity ap­pli­ca­tions.

What other fac­tors dis­tin­guishes python be­sides sim­ple gram­mar have been uti­lized to in­ter­act with is­sues such as sched­ul­ing fail­ure re­quest for your ma­chine ser­vice in just sec­onds be­cause the load fol­low­ing how the role of do­main guys emaild Osea.. I Hate syn­tax hard w

Programs that use LLMs with sta­tis­ti­cal sam­plers de­grade at longer con­text sizes partly for this rea­son. Over time, the er­ror in the ran­dom­ness builds un­til the model can no longer pro­duce log­i­cal text.

How can we mit­i­gate this new prob­lem?

Nucleus Sampling

Nucleus sam­pling is just like sta­tis­ti­cal sam­pling, but with a de­ﬁned limit to how un­likely a word is al­lowed to be.

To il­lus­trate the process, let’s set a limit (0.95) and go through each step.

WordProbabilityhat0.9bat0.05ra­di­a­tor0.04…0.01

Before we can do any­thing, we need to pro­duce our“nucleus”. To do this, we step through each item in our prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion. While do­ing so, we keep track of the cu­mu­la­tive prob­a­bil­ity, just like in sta­tis­ti­cal sam­pling. If we en­counter any words whose cu­mu­la­tive prob­a­bil­ity is greater than our limit (that is, ∑n=1xpn>0.95\sum_{n = 1}^{x} p_n > 0.95∑n=1x​pn​>0.95) we dis­card it.

After that, we are left with a new list of“probabilities”:

WordProbabilityhat0.9bat0.05

Except, these are not quite prob­a­bil­i­ties. After all, the do not add up to 1.0. Let’s ﬁx that by ap­ply­ing a soft­max to the col­lec­tion. I will not go into great de­tail of how that works. To put it sim­ply, a soft­max turns a col­lec­tion of num­bers into a proper prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion that sums to 1.0.

WordProbabilityhat0.7bat0.3

From here, we just ap­ply nor­mal sta­tis­ti­cal sam­pling to our new prob­a­bil­ity dis­tri­b­u­tion.

To sum it up, nu­cleus sam­pling the same as sta­tis­tic sam­pling, but we re­move all the most un­likely words from the dis­tri­b­u­tion ﬁrst.

Nucleus sam­pling mit­i­gates all the down­sides of the ﬁrst two al­go­rithms, while re­main­ing per­for­mant. Text is gen­er­ally free of un­nec­es­sary rep­e­ti­tion, and it avoids the ran­dom in­ser­tion of low-prob­a­bil­ity words.

Conclusion

There are a few more salient sam­pling al­go­rithms that per­haps should be in­cluded in to­day’s post, like DRY sam­pling, but un­for­tu­nately I am out of time. I’ve cov­ered the more com­mon ones to­day. Most com­mer­cial apps use nu­cleus sam­pling. Some more niche apps use a kind of greedy sam­pling. Know­ing which to use is an im­por­tant de­ci­sion. Make it wisely.

“Getting off the Modernization Treadmill”

2026-10-08

My notes from this talk by Alexander Petros at Big Sky DevCon 2026.

Alex starts by noting how “modernize” used to mean something along the lines of “update this thing that was made before I was born”. But now “modernize” means something more like “update this thing from 5-10 years ago” (hence the framing of the talk, the “modernization treadmill”).

Using a real-world example of an incredibly slow website that was required to access state-sponsored programs for welfare, Alex points out the disparity in conditions between those of us who make software and those who have to use them:

The people who develop these websites are usually doing so on high-powered internet connections and high-powered devices, but they're not using them in the conditions that the people who most need those benefits are going to be.

Then he shows a Reddit thread where somebody essentially posted, “I’m having problems with this website. I’ve been waiting for months for my application to go through. Any suggestions?” And one Reddit user responded, “The best thing you can do is go into the physical office, get a case worker, and your problems will be solved within the hour.”

The irony.

I guess we've come full circle now. It used to be:

“Don’t talk to anybody. It’s faster and more convenient to use the website!”

But now it’s:

“Don’t use the website. It’s faster and more convenient to talk to somebody!”

Have we failed at making websites?

And is our failure, at least in part, rooted in the fact that we don’t leverage the basic tools for making websites: HTML, CSS, and (in a distant third) JavaScript?

Alex goes on to argue that the technologies of the web have an ideological bent and, if used as designed, can solve so many of the performance, accessibility, and usability issues that plague so many websites.

The grain of the web’s technologies are rooted in these values:

  • User-friendly
  • Backwards- and forwards-compatibility
  • Long-term viability
  • Universal accessibility

Which means if you use them as intended, they are optimized to deliver outcomes rooted in those same values.

So if you like those values and you want those outcomes, use the platform.

Take HTML, for example. Here’s Alex:

HTML does [performance improvements] for you for free. If you've coded your website in a proper, semantical, structure HTML style, it will just get better over time at zero cost to the people who built that website

HTML is your friend. HTML won’t give you up or let you down. HTML will make it difficult for you to make a bad website.

Write it in to the requirements of the project you’re doing that it work without JavaScript. Not necessarily that it doesn’t have any JavaScript, but just that the core functionality of the website can happen without JavaScript. If you do this […] you will find that it’s very hard to deliver a bad web page because the structure that HTML requires is one that fundamentally is good for the user, performant, and cost effective.

Technologies are imbued with culture, which influences what you do and how you do it. If you can align your ideological beliefs with your technological choices, you might end up with an outcome that aligns with your values — who would’ve thought, eh?

A lot of modern software developers come from websites like Facebook, they come from big tech companies [who] fundamentally have a different set of priorities. Their job is to keep you on the website as long as possible so that you consume more ads. But that’s the opposite set of requirements and priorities that the government needs to be doing, which is to build something that is clean, quick, efficient, and gets you in and out as fast as possible. So [I tell people] that the technology they use comes from [an] ideological place. But there are different ideological places that produce different technological results and if we start from those through lines then we can produce services that help people who need them.

The ideological principles of the web are well established: users over everything else.

If you use HTML as much as possible, you’ll make something that’s as user-friendly as possible on the web.

A Newsletter of Humorous Writing #464

2026-10-08

For September 30-October 6, 2026

Hello and welcome to A Newsletter of Humorous Writing, a roundup of the week's finest short humor pieces and funny articles, and a celebration of the fantastic writers who wrote them. We have one update and one correction:

Jiji Lee wrote in about to tell us about her piece that we shared a few issues ago. We were curious if Jiji was a tennis fan, and turns out she is: “You guys aced it! I had some deep cuts at first (the long lines at Court 17…iykyk) but I wanted my details to be accessible, and crossed my fingers that there were other Pat LaFrieda stans out there.” Write using the niche specifics that are closest to you!

And the link in the Brian's Old Favorite last week was thoroughly busted. The Big Jewel has been defunct for a while, and we’re sorry if we connected you to a very unhumorous international casino site. Fortunately the Internet Archive has Dan Caprera’s piece backed up! We swear this new link is legit.

What We Enjoyed This Week

I’m Starting to Suspect That the F.D.A. Is Just Trying to Get Me to Cook by Greg Mania (The New Yorker) This is a clever premise: Greg starts with a topical observation, but writes with an eye towards the evergreen. The jokes focus more on the emotional response and reaction of the narrator, which is always a great choice for humor.

A Forty-Two-Year-Old Man Checks the Score of a High School Football Game by Aaron Hertzog (McSweeney’s) Speaking of emotion and reaction, this piece is a fun example of an internal monologue. Aaron plays with self-judgement in really fun ways here: the way the character berates himself for things that only exist inside his head are very funny.

The Return of Dirtbag Catullus by Daniel Lavery (The Chatner) We’re big Daniel fans, and his attention to detail and unabashed embrace of a nerdy reference (here an ancient Roman poet) is inspiring. Write using the niche specifics that are closest to you!

-- AD --

Come celebrate new comedy craft book INSIDE JOKES: A COMEDY AND CREATIVITY GUIDE FOR ALL WRITERS at the NY launch event, presented by A Great Week for Women! Featuring writers and performers Alexandra Petri, Emily Flake, JiJi Lee, Jennie Egerdie, book co-author Caitlin Kunkel, and more, experience INSIDE JOKES: LIVE! at Caveat on Sunday, 10/25 at 2:30pm. $5 admission, books available for purchase on site.

(Do you have an ad you'd like to place in the Newsletter? Fill out this form! )

An Old Favorite

The 6 Worst Chairs by Dayna Evans (Eater) I think about this piece every time I’m uncomfortable in a restaurant or a bar. The attention to how each chair compels a certain posture is a great vehicle for jokes. A hater masterpiece.

Do you have an Old Favorite of your own? Let us know by filling out this form and we may run your pick in a future edition of the newsletter.

Updates From Your Editors and Friends of the Newsletter

Nothing from us this week! Too busy trying to get back some of the money we blew on that international casino site.

Other Humorous Writing News

An alarming new report from Nieman Lab found that ChatGPT is stealing real New Yorker cartoonists’ signatures and adding them to faux-toons:

[Cartoonist Brendan] Loper already knew his work was “out there, getting harvested for all of this [AI] training,” he said. But an image generator faking his signature felt more personal. “I’m not a territorial person, but my name is my name. It felt very much like a violation of my personhood.”

Add this to the already massive file of evidence that AI sucks. One small silver lining: Nieman Lab commissioned a new comic from Loper about this whole debacle.

The awards will allow Mitchell Guttman (left), professor of biology, and Markus Meister (PhD '87), the Anne P. and Benjamin F. Biaggini Professor of Biological Sciences, to build a better platform for developing antibodies and to discover how the brain organizes human behavior, respectively.

Caltech and AIM Build AI Platform with Mathematicians for Mathematicians

The new tool aims to organize, synthesize, and facilitate mathematical work without losing track of the more human aspects of the mathematical process.

Alireza Marandi Named a Moore Experimental Physics Investigator

The funding will help Marandi continue to explore the generation and manipulation of quantum states at ultrafast timescales.

"Quantum does not replace the science we do, it unlocks it. Sharper sensors find exoplanets and read their atmospheres. Better clocks hold navigation together when GPS is unavailable. Secure links carry the data back from deep space."

Maria Spiropulu, Caltech's Shang-Yi Ch'en Professor of Physics, is a world-renowned leader in quantum networking: using the laws of quantum physics to connect quantum devices to each other, whether those devices are processors, sensors, or clocks. These networks offer security certified by physics rather than by mathematics and timing that holds when GPS is jammed or unavailable.

Building a Safety Layer for Humanoid Robots

Researchers in Aaron Ames's AMBER Lab at Caltech are developing the safety layer for humanoid robots—a way of mathematically guaranteeing such robots will operate safely in the real world, avoiding people and even objects that are thrown at them.

Did You Know?

A newly released panorama captured by NASA's Curiosity rover offers the most detailed view yet of distant wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission's scientists have long been waiting to see up close. Tmux Session Extension for Nova editor

2026-10-08

A Nova extension that keeps your terminals running in a tmux session per project, shared between Nova’s terminal and Ghostty, iTerm, kitty or Terminal.

Why?

With the this setup, each project gets a session and each Nova terminal tab gets a tmux window. Close a tab or quit Nova and your shells, builds and other processes keep running. Open another tab to return to an unused window, or join the session from your external terminal.

tmux also provides renamable sessions, split panes, windows and searchable scrollback inside Nova’s terminal.

Usage

Invoke via Extensions > Tmux Session, or search in the Command Palette:

  • Open in External Terminal — opens this project’s session in your terminal app
  • Copy Join Command — copies a command to join the session from another terminal
  • Show All Sessions… — lists every running session, to open, copy, rename or end one
  • Rename Session… — gives this project’s session a new name
  • End Session… — ends this project’s session and everything running in it

Get it now

You can install it in Nova Extensions Library, or from the web at: extensions.panic.com/extensions/com.gingerbeardman/com.gingerbeardman.TmuxSession/

Steven Lukes, The Diversity of Morals

2026-10-08

In August I was a discussant on a panel about Steven Lukes’s recent book, The Diversity of Morals. Here’s an extended version of what I said. A PDF version is available as well.

The Diversity of Morals asks the questions philosophers ask about morality: what is “the moral”? How wide and deep is its diversity? Is there a standpoint from which we can make our judgments? It then refuses to answer them by philosophical methods alone. Instead, it draws on the resources of both social theory and the social sciences, from primatology and anthropology to sociology and political science, in an effort to construct a defensible answer. I do not think it quite succeeds. But I am also unsure of what success would look like.

Before any critique, let me state the argument as I understand it. I confess that I found it a little tricky to reconstruct because of the way the book lays things out. The text is dense with quotations, sometimes quite lengthy, and prefers to proceed by picking out representatives of the various positions investigated, letting us hear them speak, and maybe selecting some piece of their argument to be partially endorsed and carried forward. It reminded me of being in an expertly-taught graduate seminar where the participants are working their way through a wide literature. In a seminar we would be able to stop at many points to discuss each new contributor’s ideas, to make connections in an expanding web of ideas. But because this is a book, at times it was a little too much like a whistle-stop tour of other people’s views. I found myself wanting a clearer sense of the author’s own argument. To be fair, Lukes acknowledges early on that he does not always take sides, and that sometimes “such reluctance may be the appropriate way to recognize the sheer difficulty of reaching a convincing conclusion” (xii).1

Hume, Herder, and Smith

There is a positive line of argument, though. The book argues that the word “moral” names not a domain or perspective sitting alongside the legal, economic, or political, but the standpoint from which all such standpoints are judged. It’s the point of view from which we ask what the most serious, central things in life are. There is no “outside” to this standpoint. The unmaskers of morality, from Thrasymachus to Bernard Williams, are moralists in spite of themselves. The distinctively human capacity underlying it is “Smithian empathy”, that is, an effort to understand others embedded in a second-person point of view where we both demand and owe justification. This perspective-taking is not the Humean “contagion” that we share with other primates, but a kind of projection that triangulates what you would feel, what you should feel, and what an impartial “anyone” would feel (58-62; 71-3).

This Smithian empathy is used to overcome the broad contrast that the book starts out with. On the philosophical, or Humean, side is the intuition that there can be correct answers to moral questions, possibly grounded in the conviction that people are in the end all very much the same, perhaps thanks to some intrinsic human nature. On the social-scientific, or Herderian, side is the intuition that the sheer heterogeneity of moral beliefs and practices across societies makes a nonsense of efforts to derive and defend some general substantive morality. The best we can do is document its variety, and perhaps try to naturalistically explain its origins in particular cases.

This broad distinction, as the book itself makes clear, breaks down almost immediately. There are plenty of error-theorists and moral nihilists in philosophy. And in the social sciences, there is a lot of good empirical work on the most general aspects of “moral” social behavior, which generally means the emergence of generalized exchange, or altruism, or “pro-sociality”. A little more narrowly, and where many sociologists land, we have examinations of the character “moral” beliefs or actions, of “values” of all kinds and the practices or norms associated with them. These are all “social” morals, in the book’s terminology.

The Diversity of Morals agrees that the natural and social sciences can explain the emergence and persistence of morals in that second sense, but argues that they cannot naturalistically explain the universalization of morals—what the book calls “critical” morals. This is both the expansion of moral concern past every boundary of group and culture, and an evaluative attitude toward the moral perspective itself. It seems to be a contingent historical achievement. The book explores its possible sources in Axial-age reflexivity, Enlightenment dignity, and the Durkheimian sacralization of the individual in general, even as it is repeatedly threatened by counter-sacralizations that confine empathy to the bounds of nation, volk, race, or party. Here the question is how we should think about this critical moral capacity.

For Lukes, “values” are what are important, desirable, and justifiable to ourselves and others (137). The extreme test of the relation between merely social and properly critical morals is atrocities like the Holocaust and other genocides. The book resists the “situationist consensus” that says anyone in that particular situation would have acted in those ways (99-110). But it also insists that we cannot let ourselves off the hook by saying that what went on in the minds of the people who perpetrated these atrocities is completely severed from our own morality. We need a “bridgehead” of recognizable motivation or shared rationality (116). Smithian empathy has to apply here, too, somehow.

The book finds its way out with the help of the empirical literature (from Schwartz and D’Andrade) finding that personal values vary surprisingly little across societies. Practices differ, because “what counts as” realizing shared values differs widely, but the values themselves do not. And so we end with two claims. Morals narrow along a continuum from “mere” conventions to ultimate values, with the latter being more shared than might first appear. Morals also deepen, not in the sense of becoming richer or more fruitful, but in the way the ocean deepens into utter darkness: morals deepen into non-recognition, where the second-person standpoint, the need to justify one’s values to others, fails or falls away, and the moral community shrinks to the like-minded, to tribalism. While never losing its essentially sober outlook, the book does try to end somewhat optimistically, by arguing that contemporary political polarization might be successfully overcome. Much of it, Lukes suggests, is largely manufactured non-recognition rather than truly irreconcilable differences in values.

Width and Abstraction

My first worry is that the “width” thesis is an artifact of abstraction due to measurement. The claim that value diversity is narrow rests principally on D’Andrade’s study and the Schwartz surveys (D’Andrade, 2008; Schwartz & Bardi, 2001). Across the United States, Japan, and Vietnam, and across dozens of national samples, people affirm strikingly similar hierarchies of thin value-words. We all value responsibility, honesty, self-fulfillment, treating human life as precious. Within-society variation dwarfs between-society variation. The puzzle of why practices differ so much more than values is then solved with Searle’s formula: societies differ over what counts as realizing values they share (Searle, 2010).

As the book itself notes in Chapter 1, however, Nelson Goodman points out that similarity is relative to context. Whether two things count as being alike depends on what we are looking for. If we describe values thinly enough, everything converges to similarity. Every society values “responsibility”, every society values “care”. But this is not a discovery about the true shallowness of moral disagreement, it’s a feature of the level of description we are operating at. If all the moral action is in the specification—if what responsibility is, what it demands, whom it covers, is what different cultures differ on—then the formula “shared values, divergent realizations” is not an explanation of their disagreement. It is a redescription of it.

Take the book’s own abortion example. We are told both sides agree on the values of responsibility, privacy, and self-determination, and differ only in how these are linked to the world. But these rival “conceptions” of responsibility have such different practical implications that they might as well be simply rival values. The survey data can’t really arbitrate between these readings, because the surveys only ever ask about the thin word. The work of Jerolmack & Khan (2014), which the book cites approvingly, insists that values must be viewed in context, tied to norms and practices. But the book’s claims about width rely on a process of decontextualization that it elsewhere disapproves of. The book does offer “intelligibility” and “seriousness” as a means of bounding the space of valid values. But even here, it admits that an awful lot can be left over, especially if we take the time to understand why something seemingly unintelligible or unserious at first blush might turn out to be just the opposite on further reflection. Moreover, even if these criteria can delineate a space of values it doesn’t follow that this space is small. And the optimistic parts of the Coda, the parts about about deliberation and polarization, need that space to be small, rather than a large field of genuine and irreconcilable conflict. How confident are we that that the range of real value diversity is narrow?

Depth and Disagreement

A version of this question arises in the case of the depth of values, too. By the end of the book, depth is redefined as non-recognition, as an accidental or deliberate failure of Smithian empathy. But I wonder if that is what deep value conflict meant to Isaiah Berlin and Max Weber, the value pluralists discussed in Chapter 5. For Weber, at least, deep value conflict was intractability given mutual recognition. The method of verstehen is very close to the practice of Smithian empathy. The Christian of the Sermon on the Mount and the man of worldly honor, in Weber’s example, are not failing to take up each other’s second-person standpoint. The ethic of conviction and the ethic of responsibility are held by people who share a great deal in common. Weber’s claim was that the conflict between them cannot be resolved, only decided. That is the old, frightening sense of depth: irreconcilable differences among people who recognize one another, and reject what they see.

The book puts its redefinition of depth as non-recognition to work in Chapter 4, with some success. And it is necessary in the Coda as well. But I wonder whether substituting it for the old concept discreetly retires the question the old concept named. Are there rationally irresolvable conflicts among values that remain fully mutually intelligible, among people who fully recognize each other’s standing? If the answer is yes, that is, if some conflicts survive recognition, complete information, and scrupulous Smithian empathy, then deliberation, however well designed, will not dissolve them. It can only stage them. That is Weber’s position, and I do not think the book confronts it.

Chapter 5 ends with a contrast between thinking of values as merely trade-offs (Berlin), opportunity costs within choice-sets, or truly sacrifices between incommensurable ends (Weber). The Coda returns us to that question. If the depth of morality just is non-recognition, restoring recognition through some method of deliberation seems to solve the problem of depth simply by definition. In that case, experiments in deliberation aren’t just encouraging, they’re guaranteed to work. That can’t be right. If we observe preference moderation under conditions of accountability, we can interpret that as the discovery of shared values. But this is also compatible with the softening of positions that people were never deeply invested in, while genuinely deep conflicts—deep in the Weberian sense—remain untouched. The Irish case of Citizens Assemblies cited in the Coda is indeed encouraging. But, even there, one can read the Citizens’ Assembly as an already-shared value of responsibility being jointly renegotiated, or as one side prevailing under procedural conditions favorable to it.

Solving all these problems is easier the more common ground you share. The general “anyone” of Smithian empathy, the “impartial spectator”, is one way those shared values can be smuggled into the argument. The impartial spectator’s views must come from somewhere. If we disagree, and try to empathize with one another, and your impartial spectator shares many of the same views as mine, our chances of moral agreement will be much higher. If our impartial spectators seem to differ a great deal, though, things will go much worse. Again, there is some acknowledgment of this in the book. For instance, a note quoting a communication from Samuel Fleischacker, remarks that while we need to posit a “perspective-free impartiality” in order to get Smithian empathy off the ground, “We don’t need to say we have actually achieved such impartiality”, just “hold it out as a possibility to which we aspire” (224).

Metaethics and Sacralization

The author’s own values seem clear in the book. I think I share most of them. He sides with a liberal naturalism over its various rivals, with Smith over Hume on empathy, with de Swaan and Geras over the situationists and Rorty, and so on. One place the book conspicuously does not choose is between Berlin and Weber, that is, on the question of what values are, and what it really means for them to be plural. This is a hard question for the philosophers, of course, but also for social scientists who want a meaningful link between the research they do and the values they espouse.

Consider, for example, the question of the sacralization of the person. That is, the question of how the equal dignity of all humans became, in Durkheim’s sense, sacred. Critical morals (in the book’s sense) and human rights rest on that sacralization. Was its development a discovery about human beings? Or was it a contingent, collective representation that one tribe (our own) successfully consecrated? The book’s normative voice often sounds like it wants to pick the first option. It’s a discovery. Himmler’s justifications at Poznan are a failure, even an obscenity. The rescuers were right. Bezalel Smotrich’s standpoint is moral only in the anthropological sense. The counter-sacralizers and tribalists and Schmittians are wrong. And so on. Moral universalism thus has an authority that outruns its genealogy.

Durkheim, whom Lukes knows better than anyone, plainly says it’s the second. These sacralized beliefs about human dignity are, in the end, a contingent collective representation that grew out of an advancing division of labor. He says this even as he believes that the cult of the individual is something we should be committed to and take advantage of for the purposes of social policy. In its much more bleakly Nietzschean way, Weber’s view is on this side of the argument as well. Value commitments can have deep consequences for social organization, and this is why theory begins by trying to understand why people act from their own point of view. But in the end those values are not discoveries, they are primordial commitments.

This makes for a persistent tension in sociology as a discipline. Different wings of the field do of course want to advocate for particular moral views, or views with a moral element. Sometimes it’s by way of a focus on practical advocacy or policy reform, where the model of advocacy rests on claims to substantive expertise. Sometimes it explicitly rests on some standpoint, where MacIntyre’s “prison of our own upbringing” (MacIntyre, 2013) is reimagined as a source of wisdom and insight. More grandly, though these days less often, it’s by way of a claim to have grasped—and to speak for—where history itself is going. But, as a discipline, sociology is largely defined by the insight that morality as such is downstream of contingent social facts. Again, not everyone in the field agrees. But when sociologists want to emphasize what is most distinctive about their own disciplinary perspective, for the most part they reach for classics that emphasize the historical contingency of social structure, the immense diversity of social forms, and the dreaded “sociological imagination” that allegedly allows us to connect both to individual experience. In this emphasis on the variability and historicity of social life the field tends to side with anthropology (and of course disciplinary history), rather than with philosophy and economics.

When it comes to developing a position on these matters, as opposed to preferring not to think about them, The Diversity of Morals is a very useful book because it brings out just how difficult the terrain is underfoot, and just how little we have to stray from well-trodden paths in order to get bogged down trying to coherently and defensibly answer questions about the nature of morality as such, and how it relates to the findings and practice of social science. In the end, the book knows it cannot answer its biggest questions. Lukes remarks more than once that some disputes are better continued than resolved. Perhaps that is the best we can do: to at least keep talking, in a civilized manner. I will claim one extended quotation of my own. I am reminded, a little absurdly, of a scene from At the Villa of Reduced Circumstances, Alexander McCall Smith’s gentle comedy of academic manners. The scene is a ceremonial dinner at Cambridge:

The Master then rose to give a short address. ‘Dear guests of the College,’ he began, ‘dear Fellows, dear undergraduate members of this Foundation: William de Courcey was cruelly beheaded by those who could not understand that it is quite permissible for rational men to differ on important points of belief or doctrine. The world in which he lived had yet to develop those qualities of tolerance of difference of opinion which we take for granted, but which we must remind ourselves is of rather recent creation and is by no means assured of universal support. There are amongst us still those who would deny to others the right to hold a different understanding of the fundamental issues of our time. Thus, if we look about us we see people of one culture or belief still at odds with their human neighbours who are of a different culture or belief; and we see many who are prepared to act upon this difference to the extent of denying the humanity of those with whom they differ. … ‘Here in this place of learning, let us remind ourselves of the possibility of combating, in whatever small way we can, those divisions that come between man and man, between woman and woman, so that we may recognise in each other that vulnerable humanity that informs our lives, and makes life so precious; so that each may find happiness in his or her life, and in the lives of others. For what else is there for us to hope for? What else, I ask you, what else?’ (McCall Smith, 2003, pp. 56–57)

What else, indeed. Almost all of the people in these conversations are committed to something like the universalization story in their everyday lives, whether its origins lie in Axial transcendence, Kantian dignity under the shadow of God, Hans Joas’s soul and gift, Durkheimian sacredness, or something else. Philosophical error theorists and moral nihilists do not, on the whole, want to live in a state of vicious anarchy. The same goes for academic Marxists, debunking Evolutionary Psychologists, hopelessly confused Critical Realists, biogenomic bean-counters, Scandinavian DBO enumerators, tradition-marinaded MacIntyreans, authenticity-obsessed standpoint epistemologists, and have-your-cake-and-eat-it pragmatists. All of them are people you are likely to encounter at conferences. They are all in some sense already in the same conversation as you. But the problem, in the end, is that you have to make peace with your enemies, not your friends.

References

D’Andrade, R. (2008). A study of personal and cultural values: American, Japanese, and Vietnamese. London: Palgrave Macmillan.

Jerolmack, C., & Khan, S. (2014). Talk is cheap: Ethnography and the attitudinal fallacy. Sociological Methods & Research, 43(2), 178–209.

Lukes, S. (2025). The diversity of morals. Princeton: Princeton University Press.

MacIntyre, A. (2013). On having survived the academic moral philosophy of the twentieth century. In F. O’Rourke (Ed.), What happened to and in moral philosophy in the twentieth century (pp. 17–34). Notre Dame, IN: University of Notre Dame Press.

McCall Smith, A. (2003). At the villa of reduced circumstances. Edinburgh: Polygon.

Schwartz, S., & Bardi, A. (2001). Value hierarchies across cultures: Taking a similarities perspective. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 32(3), 268–290.

Searle, J. (2010). Making the Social World: The Structure of Human Civilization. New York: Oxford University Press.

32 years and still diggin!

2026-10-07, updated: 2026-10-10

On 10/7/1994, I wrote my first blog post.

I've been blogging ever since.

In the first years when wifi wasn't in every hotel room and restaurant as it is today, before cell phones or even iPods, there were weekly lapses when I went on vacation or to a massage retreat in the middle of nowhere.

Or in 2002 when I had life-saving heart surgery. I was gone for a week then. But as soon as I got home, I added a post so people knew I was okay. I understood that I was missed, and appreciated that. ;-)

But other than those week-long lapses, I'm pretty sure I've blogged every day since. I am what you would call a Natural Born Blogger. I got the blogging bug.

We've done a lot on this blog, it's hard to sum up. We created things that had lasting value. Told the truth about what the tech industry was up to, from the point of view of a Silicon Valley insider (me) who knows the language, where most journalists are intimidated. We fought the big companies and won. Podcasting was created in the community defined by this blog in the early 00s, and it remains independent to this day.

The bigs declared RSS dead, another product of this community. Wishful thinking perhaps, but things like RSS don't die. It's not like that. You can't create a better format for a standard. All the competition RSS has ever received, just changed the names of things, that's not competition, that's being petty.

I think we're on the verge of having new relevance, it feels that way because my secret weapon, Frontier, is running again and it will get even stronger and fit in better, now that I've been working primarily in JavaScript for the last 13 years. Today we're adding Node-like packages and support for WebSockets. Last time we worked on this, neither of those existed.

I take blogging seriously, you should too. It's very powerful, as long as we're really working on the web. There's a difference between having a product you can access through a browser and being on the web.

Small pieces loosely joined. All parts replaceable. Never forget that. If you can't plug in replacements for any component, if one piece gets too large to replicate, you should hit the Back button, as Google says you should do on my blog.

Why are they trying to destroy the historic record about the web on the web itself? I have no idea. Certainly they must have had some discussion internally, or with their partner at the EFF about the cost of destroying so much history. Usually when a platform vendor is going to break you, you get invited to a private meeting where you can tell them the cost and beg them not to do it. Not with Google.

And, as they say --

Still diggin!

Pluralistic: Disloyalty (07 Oct 2026)

2026-10-07, updated: 2026-10-09

Today's links Disloyalty: Air Canada's frequent flier fuckery. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Indie booksellers v internet; Coke pays dieticians to astroturf soda taxes; Voting in a voter-suppression state; Facebook v your use of Facebook. Upcoming appearances: Hudson, Calgary, Winnipeg, Paris, Vancouver, Victoria, Ottawa, Kilkenny, Sheffield, Oxford, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. Disloyalty (permalink) Up until very recently indeed, airlines were the only businesses that I dealt with regularly that practiced "price discrimination," charging different customers different prices for the same seats. Economists broadly like this "second-order" price discrimination, where a company charges customers different prices based on the circumstances of the purchase, such as a bakery discounting bread at the end of the day. When an airline cranks up the price of an itinerary that doesn't include a Saturday stay, they're using that fact as a proxy for "price-insensitive" business travelers whose bosses can afford to pay more for a ticket, rather than paying a worker overtime to spend a weekend away from home after a meeting. Despite the arguments about "efficiency," it's safe to say that *fliers* hate this. The airlines' pricing algorithms are so opaque and capricious that anyone who buys a ticket at *any* price inevitably feels like they got a bad deal. This situation is only exacerbated by the airlines' extreme and aggressive secrecy over their pricing strategies, which includes lawsuits against websites that use historical pricing data to predict when a plane ticket will be the cheapest to buy: https://www.eff.org/document/preliminary-injunction-american-airlines-v-farechase-inc When a company wants the government to intervene to prohibit third parties from publishing factual information about its prices, that's a bad look. Hard to believe that they're so sure that you, the customer, will be delighted by these pricing tactics that they can't bear to have these third parties ruin the surprise. But this second-order discrimination is *so* 20th century. Here in the 21st century, we have *first-order* price discrimination, in which AI-powered pricing algorithms use commercial surveillance data about *you*, personally, to predict the highest price you're willing to pay. In this world of "surveillance pricing," every traveler (or customer) sees a different price, in a kind of cod-Marxist dystopia whose motto is "from each according to their ability (to pay), to each according to their (desperate) needs": https://pluralistic.net/2025/01/11/socialism-for-the-wealthy/#rugged-individualism-for-the-poor Airlines *love* this kind of pricing, and they have means, motive and opportunity to practice it. All over the world, airlines have acquired or entered into joint ventures with surveillance pricing companies. These deals put the airlines on the horns of a dilemma: they love to boast to their shareholders about the way that surveillance pricing will let them gouge fliers, but inevitably the public finds out about these investor calls and breaks out the pitchforks and torches. This triggers embarrassing climbdowns, like Delta's fiasco of summer 2025, when CEO Ed Bastian bragged to shareholders that his deal with the Israeli surveillance pricing company Fetcherr would boost profits by 50% (!) by figuring out which customers could be safely gouged. When fliers, civil society groups and members of Congress got wind of this and raised a ruckus, Fetcherr publicly disavowed Bastian's remarks, insisting that it wasn't even capable of the kind of price-fixing he'd promised. Then Delta launched a smear campaign against its critics, claiming that Bastian never said the thing he *absolutely said* and accusing surveillance pricing activists of peddling "misinformation": https://groundworkcollaborative.org/news/amid-deltas-ai-pricing-scheme-groundwork-applauds-congressional-action-to-crack-down-on-surveillance-pricing-schemes/ Meanwhile, airlines all over the world have quietly switched their frequent flier reward programs from "mileage-based" rewards to "revenue-based" rewards. That means that you get points and status based on how much you spend on your ticket, not how far you fly. What may not be obvious from this move is that it forces frequent fliers to buy their tickets directly from the airlines, who claim that they can't tell how much you've spent on your ticket otherwise. So tickets bought on sites like Expedia or through travel agents often qualify for insultingly small points awards, or no points at all. For example, British Airways once gave me *12 points* on a $2,000 Alaska Air ticket because I didn't buy it through British Airways' site (attaining BA's gold status requires *50,000* points). Forcing frequent fliers to buy their tickets directly from the airline's website sets things up beautifully for surveillance-driven, first-order price discrimination. Airlines you do business with regularly can augment the personal information you provide to them and the data they collect from you with sensitive information purchased from the unregulated data-broker industry, which will cheerfully disclose your salary, credit card debts, or even if you've recently lost a parent and might be flying out for a funeral. The airlines strenuously deny that they're doing this, of course, but they continue to make investor-facing announcements about their exciting deals with surveillance pricing companies…and things are getting *weird* for frequent travelers. Thanks to a lot of book-related travel over the past couple of years, I have "Elite" status with Air Canada. Yesterday, I needed to book a last-minute, one-way fare on a route that is only serviced by Air Canada (AC enjoys a monopoly over many Canadian routes, even between major Canadian cities). I checked it out on Google Flights and found a fare for the eye-watering sum of USD829.73. Now, my normal daily-use browser is Firefox, but I know from long experience that I can't log in to my Air Canada frequent flier account on any browser except Chromium, which I keep installed on my system for just this kind of hostile garbage website. So I tabbed over to Chromium and pasted the Google Flights outbound link that would take me to a pre-populated reservation form on aircanada.com. To my amazement, that same flight was showing as a USD1200 fare! These were identical trips, loaded via identical referrer URLs. The difference was that in the browser where Air Canada knew that I was an extremely loyal and prolific customer, they had whacked me with a *44.8% premium* to punish me for my loyalty! I couldn't believe it. I actually called Air Canada's customer service line for "Elite" fliers, and the customer service rep was at a loss for an explanation and could only apologise and suggest that I write a letter to the company. I'm publishing this instead, because a) this will do more to punish Air Canada for trying to screw me over; and b) this can help you book your tickets in the future. Yesterday, I finished buying the ticket in my logged-out Firefox window (Air Canada's website will work with Firefox to buy tickets provided you don't try to log in to your Aeroplan account first), paying $829. Then I flipped back to Chromium, where I was still logged into my Air Canada Aeroplan account, located the reservation, and added my frequent flier number to it. I guess this is how I'm buying my plane tickets from now on. via Michael Tsai

Apple’s App Icon HOA

2026-10-06

Louie Mantia has a great post about how app icons are converging towards the squircle on iOS and macOS.

His post reads like a history. If you’re wondering, “How did we get to a place where all app icons are becoming squircles?” Mantia’s post answers that question by starting at the beginning.

It’s hard to walk away from Mantia’s article without a sense of empathy for Apple’s position, like “Oh ok, I get why they’re doing what they’re doing. It makes sense.”

Apple’s direction is kind of a tacit acknowledgement to how most people are shipping app icons. Apple is “paving the cowpaths” as it were, because most app icons are just brand logos.

Nowadays, it’s these bland, big-business logo icons that make up a good chunk of iOS Home Screens and macOS Docks, instead of the beautiful, illustrative app icons that used to dominate our devices.

So many app icons are just logos in a squircle, so Apple made tools like the Icon Composer and glass effects to help make that approach look good by default.

Apple is helping most people most of the time make app icons that don’t suck.

[Apple is making] it easier for all apps to fit in on the platform, especially apps built by designers and developers who aren’t familiar with how to make an icon that looks great next to first-party icons.

The net effect is:

some of the platform’s best icons look worse, while some of the platform’s worst icons look better.

In other words, this new approach raises the floor but it also lowers the ceiling.

The thought that came to mind as I read Mantia’s post was, “This reminds me of HOAs.”

I grew up in a neighborhood where anyone could do anything with their homes and yards, so you had this eclectic mix throughout the neighborhood — everything from “Wow, that house is so unique!” to “That thing is a dump.”

Somewhere along the way HOAs became more prevalent (in my neck of the woods), where all the houses in a neighborhood have to meet a certain standard — and so they all start to look the same.

It keeps the dumpy things out, yet nobody stands out.

That’s kinda what macOS feels like right now with regard to app icons.

For better or worse, squircle app icons are Apple’s HOA and we’re all just living in it.
